title: Ratatouille
subtitle: Slow-cooked Provençal vegetable stew
excerpt: Aubergine, courgette, peppers, and tomatoes cooked slowly in olive oil until each vegetable is tender and the whole dish is concentrated and rich. The version where each vegetable is cooked separately before being combined makes the best ratatouille.
sourceNotes: Ratatouille is the defining summer vegetable dish of Provence and Nice. The name derives from the Occitan ratatolha and the French touiller, 'to stir'. Elizabeth David, French Provincial Cooking (1960), gives the method and stresses the importance of cooking each vegetable separately to avoid a stew of uniformly mushy vegetables. Richard Olney, Simple French Food (1974), takes this further, insisting that ratatouille must be slow-cooked and should never be watery. The dish is from the Nice tradition (ratatouille niçoise).

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze for up to 3 months. Ratatouille holds very well in the freezer and can be reheated from frozen.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Ratatouille improves on the second day. Make a day ahead and reheat gently. It is also excellent at room temperature.

content.text: The secret of a good ratatouille is cooking each vegetable separately before combining them. If all the vegetables go into the pot at once, they steam rather than fry, release their water at the same time, and produce a bland stew. When each is fried in olive oil until it has some colour and concentrated slightly, the finished dish has distinct vegetables and a full, round flavour.
This approach takes longer but is not laborious. It can be done entirely in one large pan, working in stages.

Salt the aubergine chunks and leave in a colander for 20 minutes. Squeeze dry in a clean cloth. Heat 3 tbsp oil in the large frying pan over high heat. Fry the aubergine for 8 minutes until golden on all sides. Transfer to the Dutch oven.
In the same pan with 2 tbsp oil, fry the courgettes for 5 minutes until golden. Transfer to the Dutch oven.
Fry the peppers with 2 tbsp oil for 5 minutes until softened and slightly charred at the edges. Transfer to the Dutch oven.

In the same pan with 1 tbsp oil, cook the onion over medium heat for 8 minutes until soft. Add the garlic, thyme, and bay and cook for 2 minutes. Add the tomatoes and cook for 10 minutes until thickened. Season well.

Add the tomato mixture to the Dutch oven containing the fried vegetables. Stir gently to combine. Taste and season. Cook over low heat for a further 15 minutes, uncovered, until the ratatouille is thick and concentrated. Remove the thyme and bay. Add the fresh basil just before serving.

items.cause: The vegetables were not fried separately, or the tomatoes were not cooked down enough.
items.fix: Cook uncovered over medium heat until the excess liquid evaporates. A ratatouille should be thick and rich, not soupy.

items.cause: It was added to oil that was not hot enough, so it absorbed the oil before sealing.
items.fix: The oil must be very hot before the aubergine goes in, almost smoking. Degorging the aubergine in salt beforehand also reduces its capacity to absorb oil.

items.symptom: The vegetables are all the same soft texture
items.cause: All the vegetables were cooked together rather than separately.
items.fix: The separate-cooking method is what gives ratatouille distinct vegetable textures. If the vegetables are already combined and overcooked, serve the dish as a sauce alongside pasta or grilled fish rather than as a side dish.

content.text: Ratatouille is from Nice and the surrounding Côte d'Azur. The aubergines, tomatoes, courgettes, and peppers in the dish all arrived in France from the Americas via Mediterranean trade routes and flourished in the southern climate. The dish appears in French cookery writing from the early 20th century, though similar preparations existed in Provence earlier under different names. It became well known outside France partly through the recipes of Elizabeth David and later through Julia Child.
